{{short description|Elementary function in mathematics}}
In [[number theory]], the '''Langlands–Deligne local constant''', named after [[Robert Langlands]] and [[Pierre Deligne]], also known as the '''local epsilon factor''',<ref>{{cite journal |title=Elliptic curves and local <math>\epsilon</math>-factors |last1=Kramer |first1=K. |last2=Tunnell |first2= J. |author-link2= Jerrold B. Tunnell |journal=[[Compositio Mathematica]] |volume=46 |year=1982 |issue=3 |pages=307–352 |url=https://www.numdam.org/item/CM_1982__46_3_307_0.pdf}}</ref> is a function associated with a [[representation (mathematics)|representation]] <math>\rho</math> of the [[Weil group]] of a [[local field]]. The [[functional equation]]
:<math>L(\rho,s) = \varepsilon(\rho,s)L(\rho^v,1-s)</math>
of the [[Artin L-function]] associated to <math>\rho</math> has a function <math>\varepsilon(\rho,s)</math> appearing in it, equal to a constant called the [[Artin root number]] times an [[elementary function|elementary real function]] of <math>s</math>, and Langlands discovered that <math>\varepsilon(\rho,s)</math> can be written in a canonical way as a product
:<math>\varepsilon(\rho,s) = \prod \varepsilon(\rho_v,s,\psi_v)</math>
of local constants <math>\varepsilon(\rho_v,s,\psi_v)</math> associated to primes <math>v</math>.

In [[Tate's thesis|his thesis]], [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]] proved the existence of the local constants in the case that <math>\rho</math> is one-dimensional.
[[Bernard Dwork]] proved the existence of the local constant <math>\varepsilon(\rho_v,s,\psi_v)</math> up to sign.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dwork |first=Bernard |date=1956 |title=On the Artin root number |journal=[[American Journal of Mathematics]] |volume=78 |issue=2 |pages=444–472 |doi=10.2307/2372524 |mr=0082476}}</ref>
The original proof of the existence of the local constants by {{harvtxt|Langlands|1970}} used local methods and was rather long and complicated, and never published. Deligne later discovered a simpler proof using global methods.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Deligne |first=Pierre |title=Modular Functions of One Variable II |publisher=Springer Berlin, Heidelberg |year=1973 |isbn=978-3-540-06558-6 |editor-last=Deligne |editor-first=Pierre |pages=501–597 |chapter=Les constantes des équations fonctionnelles des fonctions L |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-37855-6_7 |mr=0349635 |editor-last2=Kuyk |editor-first2=Willem}}</ref>

==Properties==

The local constants <math>\varepsilon(\rho,s,\psi_v)</math> depend on a representation <math>\rho</math> of the Weil group and a choice of character <math>\psi_E</math> of the additive group of <math>E</math>{{Clarification needed|date=April 2026}}. They satisfy the following conditions:
*If <math>\rho</math> is one-dimensional then <math>\varepsilon(\rho,s,\psi_E)</math> is the constant associated to it by Tate's thesis as the constant in the functional equation of the local L-function.
*<math>\varepsilon(\rho_1\oplus\rho_2,s,\psi_E) = \varepsilon(\rho_1,s,\psi_E)\varepsilon(\rho_2,s,\psi_E).</math>As a result, <math>\varepsilon(\rho,s,\psi_E)</math> can also be defined for virtual representations <math>\rho</math>.
*If <math>\rho</math> is a virtual representation of dimension 0 and <math>E</math> contains <math>K</math> then <math>\varepsilon(\rho,s,\psi_E) = \varepsilon(\operatorname{Ind}_{E/K} \rho, s, \psi_K)</math>.

[[Brauer's theorem on induced characters|Brauer's theorem]] on induced characters implies that these three properties characterize the local constants.

Deligne showed that the local constants are trivial for real (orthogonal) representations of the Weil group.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Deligne |first=Pierre |date=1976 |title=Les constantes locales de l'équation fonctionnelle de la fonction L d'Artin d'une représentation orthogonale |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=35 |pages=299–316 |doi=10.1007/BF01390143 |mr=0506172}}</ref>

==Notational conventions==

There are several different conventions for denoting the local constants.
*The parameter <math>s</math> is redundant and can be combined with the representation <math>\rho</math>, because ε(ρ, ''s'', ψ<sub>''E''</sub>) =  ε(ρ⊗||<sup>''s''</sup>, 0, ψ<sub>''E''</sub>) for a suitable character ||.
*Deligne includes an extra parameter <math>dx</math> consisting of a choice of Haar measure on the local field. Other conventions omit this parameter by fixing a choice of Haar measure: either the Haar measure that is self dual with respect to <math>\psi</math> (used by Langlands), or the Haar measure that gives the integers of <math>E</math> measure 1. These different conventions differ by elementary terms that are positive real numbers.
